exclusions.A: In the end the council struck a deal with the county for its standard plain letters, made a size larger because the post office asked for larger letters on the new signs.
exclusions.B: This spring the council at last replaced them with white reflective letters on green metal.
exclusions.C: The county had issued its rule on reflective letters nine years earlier, and the council filed it away and left every board where it hung.
exclusions.D: Dora Pask, the town clerk, had put the county's rule before the council every spring.

WV12-P01.4.note: To strike a deal with the county is to agree on one; nothing is crossed out, hit, halted, or suddenly realised.

exclusions.B: A street sign has one job, and Marrow's boards did it badly.
exclusions.C: The council should have taken them down the year the county's rule arrived and put up letters that a stranger can read at a glance, instead of waiting for an ambulance to prove the point.
exclusions.D: The driver mistook Lower Gate for it, as though the two boards had been swapped, and reached the house eleven minutes late.
exclusions.E: This spring the council at last replaced them with white reflective letters on green metal.

support: A street sign has one job, and Marrow's boards did it badly.
Half the boards in town were rotting at the edges, and the Gates, among the first Marrow painted, had faded to grey on cream.
WV12-P01.5.note: The author judges the boards as illegible and decaying and wishes they had come down years earlier; no statement reads as ironic in a way that would support another choice.

exclusions.B: She had cut every joint by hand from cedar, so closely that a knife blade would hardly slip between the pieces, and had sealed each roof seam with pitch she warmed on her stove until it ran like syrup.
exclusions.C: Thirty years of rain had beaten on those roofs, and the cedar beneath was still as dry and square as the day she cut it.
exclusions.D: It was in her workshop that I learned what those hives were.
exclusions.E: In August we took away the full frames, with the sound of the hives carrying in through her kitchen window.

WV12-P02.4.note: Pitch that seals seams and is warmed until it runs like syrup is a sticky resin.

exclusions.B: She still leaves the hives to look after themselves for a week each August while she visits her daughter in Lisle, and before the first frost she still climbs the ladder onto the shed roof to sweep off the leaves.
exclusions.C: Thirty years of rain had beaten on those roofs, and the cedar beneath was still as dry and square as the day she cut it.
exclusions.D: Those two hives stand against the fence to this day, and she keeps them still.
exclusions.E: I have built six hives of my own since, all to her pattern, and the best of them is a shade less square than either of hers.

support: Thirty years of rain had beaten on those roofs, and the cedar beneath was still as dry and square as the day she cut it.
I have built six hives of my own since, all to her pattern, and the best of them is a shade less square than either of hers.
WV12-P02.5.note: The narrator praises the hives' craftsmanship and durability and copies their pattern; Mrs. Pellow's dry reply about counting change concerns the narrator, not the hives, so it does not support another choice.

exclusions.A: The sun drops behind Calder Ridge, the volunteers at the church food bank lock its doors, the streetlights on the hill come on, and still the birds wheel overhead.
exclusions.B: Every September, a little before dark, the chimney swifts of Wenbury gather over the old Linden Row School.
exclusions.C: Then the church clock strikes seven, and the first swifts drop into the chimney; the last children leave the schoolyard and the last bus passes the school gates while the rest pour in after them.
exclusions.D: The first evening I watched them, I took the circling flock for smoke from the school's furnace, which has been cold for eleven years.

WV12-P04.4.note: A church food bank with volunteers who lock its doors is a store of supplies, not a financial firm, row, riverbank, or tilt.

exclusions.A: The old chimney should never have been left in this state, and the council is to blame for it.
exclusions.B: Since 1996 he has stood in the schoolyard each September evening with a hand counter, and his notebooks show the roost holding steady at about five thousand birds, as he expects it to next year.
exclusions.D: Before the swifts return in May, that stripe of cement should be cut out and redone in lime.
exclusions.E: The result is a poor repair, a stripe of grey cement from the crack to the chimney's top, so smooth that a swift's claws slide straight off it.

support: As it stands, the old chimney is a badly patched roost that wastes half its own flue.
The result is a poor repair, a stripe of grey cement from the crack to the chimney's top, so smooth that a swift's claws slide straight off it.
WV12-P04.5.note: The writer calls the chimney in its current state a badly patched, wasteful roost and assigns blame, which is disapproval (aimed largely at its repair); no ironic reading supports another choice, though a reader might note the disapproval targets the repair more than the chimney itself.
